@Hardwareunboxed  True dat, but even the gtx 1650 gddr6 was as well. Yet on laptops its performance at 50w wasn't terrible. I don't know how this rx6500xt at 50w in a laptop will be meaningfully faster than a gtx 1650 gddr6. And its got competition from the 40w to 50w rtx 3050 and rtx 3050ti.

That would place it around a rx470, which even a gtx 1650 gddr6 is basically on par with. And there's more and more portable options like the g14 packing the 60w rtx 3060's in them which really helps it out. Even in entry level gaming laptops, compared to the gtx 1650 gddr6, this rx6500m seems more like a downgrade. And I doubt it'll be cheaper than them (as in costing $600 or less).

comments.text:
They are doing it because it will sell, yes. Which is the part I am fine with. It's not something I am happy about, it is not something I will applaud AMD for, but it is also not something that I think merits any real outrage.

The main issue I have with this product is the naming — 6500 XT suggests that it is an upgrade from the 5500 XT, when in reality it's more of a sidegrade/downgrade. Also if AMD did indeed claim that they needed to cut down the feature set so severely to hit a $200 MSRP as Steve quoted, then that does indeed sound like a lie, and lies are always offensive. (Though it sounded like Steve was paraphrasing, so maybe the statement was originally phrased in a way that didn't make it literally untrue.)

But apart from that? It's just a bad product. Scores of bad products get released all the time. Sturgeon's Law: 90% of everything is crap. It is not offensive, it's just reality and probably an unavoidable one.

And this product does seem like it would at least serve some sort of purpose, if the MSRP doesn't turn out to be an utter fantasy. If you don't have a gaming PC and you want one, and you're on a fairly tight budget, and you have a PCI-e Gen4 motherboard, and you don't want to deal with the secondary market, and you want a warranty... then the sad fact is that this product may turn out to be the best option that fits those constraints, which are all fairly reasonable and plausible.

And on that basis alone I can't say this product is totally useless or pointless. There actually is a legitimate market for it.

It doesn't mean a lot to say that "under more normal market conditions" that this card is utterly pointless. That is just a thought experiment at best, or wishful thinking at worst, and not reflective of the reality we are actually living in.

You can say that people should wait to buy a graphics card until the market has settled down. I think that is decent advice, but it is not without its costs and risks; see everyone who decided to sit out the last generation of graphics cards based on the mediocre performance and price-to-performance gains.

comments.text:
This was a FANTASTIC review. Thanks for including an example of SAM. I was hesitant on whether that might save it a bit.. and sadly it does not. If it doesn't boost Assassins Creed Valhalla it is going to be as useful as tits on a fish. Also thank you for providing "settings scaling" in a handful of games.

I actually believe AMD's statement about the small die size being needed to hit a somewhat tolerable MSRP. And I know you have been exposed to at least some of the info that verifies this:  Moore's Law Is Dead had reported multiple times that GDDR6 is costing the AIBs $11-12 per GB these days. That's up from $3 per GB before the madness.... And I know you knows this since you commented on the last video where Tom did a BOM cost break-down. Taking $44-48 out of the $200 now, as opposed to $12 for the 5500XT 4GB back then changes the situation drastically..... 

This doesn't change the fact that the 6500XT sucks ass. This doesn't change the fact that going for PCIe x4 is dumb as taters. And it doesn't change the fact that AMD should have gone "ok, it's $240 but you get x8 and hardware encode".... But since You, Tech Jesus and Linus the Clown tore AMD a new one for the realistically put $380 (again, it has $88 worth of VRAM) MSRP of the 6600XT I guess they felt like they were in a no-win situation.

But we REALLY need to start talking about Nvidia's and AMD's original MSRPs vs what is being published these days. It is so boneheaded and simplistic to go "bUt ThE MsRp oF tHe 3060 iS jUsT $329 LoOk hOw gReEdy AmD iS wItH $380 FoR tHe 6600XT!!!111oneoneone"..... The 3060 has $132 worth of VRAM on it... you have to be some special kind of stupid to think this will ever happen, and IF it ever happens the 6600XT is obviously going to go for less than MSRP since it has 4GB less VRAM.

I hate this situation as much as everyone else, but if we put it upon ourselves to point fingers and place blame it is imperative that we have the facts straight.... even if this upsets the people who just want easily quotable opinions that make big corps the bad guys by default.

comments.text:
@anhiirr  I can see the temptation to see things that way, but I have to disagree. A desktop is still a much better investment if you're just going to be using it at home most of the time. Building a compact and relatively portable desktop is also not that difficult or much more expensive than building a mid-sized one.  I've seen pre-built desktop PCs with RTX 3060 ti's and 10400F CPUs for around 1100 USD in my region recently. I've seen RTX 3060's by themselves for around 420 USD recently as well. Either of those options would be a much better choice for a gaming PC, but even if you add another 200 USD on top of those prices, I still think that most people would probably be better off going with a desktop over a laptop for a gaming PC. Don't buy a laptop if you don't need it. Laptops are almost impossible to upgrade. If one component dies, it's often not even worth getting them fixed once they're past their warranty, or, at best, it's still going to be a lot more expensive than it would be to fix the same type of component on a desktop.

Desktops can be upgraded piece by piece, and are much easier to maintain (replacing fans, cleaning the dust out, etc. is very easy/ cheap). The ability to upgrade just the graphics card, or just the CPU, or just the ram, is also a huge advantage. It's also easier to get a good return on your investment with desktop components, as they don't degrade in value as much as laptops do, and that is in large part because of the fact that laptops tend to have issues or break a lot sooner than desktop PCs do. comments.text:
WOW. Just wow. What an unbelievably bad product this will be for most users. 

Most people who buy this (or at least, most people who are in the market to buy something like this) are not going to have PCI-E 4.0 support, and also aren't even going to know how much of a performance bottleneck this is going to cause, putting its performance well below an RX 5500 XT, and even well behind a 4GB RX 570 or 3GB GTX 1060. 

And... how much of a cost saving are they getting by making these with support for only 4 PCI-E lanes? As I understand it, it's quite a small cost savings, but it's going to give the card a huge performance hit on probably most systems that it will actually be used in... 

I just hope that I'm wrong, and that most people without PCI-E 4.0 support will learn about this issue and NOT buy this. 

I would also just like to mention that many B450 (AM4) boards which don't officially support PCI-E 4.0, do actually support it, but only with older bioses iirc (or maybe also with a custom, unnoficial bios, if you can even find such a thing), so if you do a little bit of research, you might find a way to get the RX 6500 XT running with PCI-E 4.0 support on older/ cheap AM4 motherboards, but you will probably be stuck not being able to update the bios, which will likely limit CPU support to Zen+ or maybe Zen 2 CPUs. To my knowledge, it's usually not feasible to revert to an older version of the bios either, so be aware. I can just imagine that some people will actually have this card working at PCI-E 4.0, but when they update their bios and lose that PCI-E 4.0 support, their graphics performance is going to suddenly become slower, and they'll likely never figure out what caused the performance hit XD

So if the 6500XT was $150 and used on a PCI-E 4.0 system, it would be OK as an RX580 replacement.  As soon as you put it on a PCI-E 3.0 system it turns to crap.

um,
so this beats the 1050 ti by a lot . The 1050 ti is $240 right now.  It also beats the 1650 which is like $330.

if this is truly $200, then let's forget the products of 5 years ago, this is the best value GPU on the market by a long way and destroys the competition for value for money.

comments.text:
As soon as I saw the specs, I was shocked at the measly 64-bit bus.  Wondering why on earth would it have such a small bus.  Hell, even the very first GPU I ever bought back in the early 2000s (ATI Radeon 9800 Pro) had a 256-bit bus.  I know a lot of midrange cards these days still work perfectly only needing 128-bit buses.  But 64?  I literally couldn't remember ever seeing a card with such a small bus.  So much so I actually had to look it up to see what other card had that small of a bus.  GT 1030 is what came up.... nuff said.

What was AMD thinking with this one?  Surely they knew that small of a bus was going to seriously hamper this card's ability to keep up with the throughput.  Is this a limitation of the laptop GPU?  Or was AMD hoping the higher bandwidth of the PCIE 4.0 interface would make up for the losses in the bus width?  Either way, that's a bad call.  Especially when AMD is well aware that PCIE 4.0 adoption is still pretty low at this point, and even more especially when many PC gamers don't have enough hardware knowledge to know at a glance what "bus width" means nor how it relates to performance.  At least not enough to recognize and relate that to the PCIE standard on their motherboard in "their" own PC.

From where I stand, this may not be "as bad" as the whole GT 1030 DDR4 fiasco Nvidia pulled, but it's still pretty bad.  Especially at this price point.  This is a midrange price point (yes I consider any card between $200-$400 midrange) for what is clearly a budget card.  What's worse, is it's a midrange price point for a card that can so easily be gimped to bottom of the barrel budget performance from something so simple as installing it in "common" PCs of today since most of the current adopted market, still have PCIE 3.0 interfaces in them.  That's not acceptable in my opinion.  And AMD shouldn't have the right to use the excuse "well it's your fault because you should've known better from the specs on the card and your PC" in this scenario.  AMD are selling this as a midrange GPU when they damn well know the vast majority of the current market would only end up getting bottom of the barrel budget performance from it.  That may not technically be false advertising.  But it sure as hell is misleading advertising.

EDIT:  Only just caught the bit about this card only being able to utilize PCIE to 4X....  (Literally just facepalmed myself and am at a complete loss for words...I honestly don't know what to say)... This card is an embarrassment.

Of course, since Moore's Law died with the 28nm node, electronics will be getting gradually more expensive with each generation.

IC will only help between GPU and VRAM, not VRAM and system, so it's effectively predictable as long as data will need to traverse the PCIe bus.

comments.text:
Today's $200 USD MSRP GPU is about what a $140 USD GPU back in 2016 - 2017 was.  Inflation has hit HARD, no one escapes it, it's global and some countries are worse than others.  So, add about 15% to the cost back in 2017 just for inflation.  Then, the largest markets for GPUs have added large import taxes since 2016.  In the EU, it's a 20 - 25% VAT that's been added, and in the US it's a 25% tariff, and this also affects Canada, as LTT talked about in Feb, 2021 but they fail to remember that when doing new videos.  That 25% tariff hit Jan 1, 2021 and the different makers of GPUs SAID their prices are going up because of it.   

The inflation is probably here to stay unless there's a global economic collapse which tends to bring deflation, but the large import taxes will go away as soon as companies move GPU manufacturing out of China.  The importers are the ones to pay these taxes, and the importers are the companies themselves, so AMD, Nvidia, ASUS, XFX, MSI, Gigabyte, etc.....   So their MSRPs have to account for those large import taxes.  I'm also assuming that since a large chunk of their sales is the EU and US, they've spread out the expense of selling GPUs over the global market

So this is similar to a $140 USD product back in 2017.  140 + 15% inflation = 160 + 25% import taxes = $200 USD.  So, what cost $140 USD back in 2017?  That would be an RX 460 and an Nvidia GTX 1050 Ti.  

So how did this compare to the GTX 1050 Ti in this video?  SUBSTANTIALLY better.

That's today's economy sorry to say, and many Youtube channels keep forgetting economics, but you can't.  The inflation over the last 2 years is more than probably the last 15 years.  I pay 150 - 200% more for many things than I did 3 years ago.  TSMC charges more money per wafer.  Every component that goes onto a GPU is more expensive.

And the 2 Steve's from GN and HDWU are the WORST at keeping all this into account.  Tim from HDWU understands this, but Steve doesn't and keeps wanting to blame the chipmakers like Nvida and AMD, but they can't sell for a loss.  They have to make a certain profit margin or they're not going to bother making the product.


APUs are going to be the thing to get, and AMD is coming out with much better APUs for Zen 4.  Those don't come out of China and don't have the large tariffs.  But Zen 4 WILL cost more due to the high inflation.  

The reality is it's going to be hard for either Nvidia or AMD to make low end GPUs and make money simply due to expectations of what the products should be, but they HAVE to cut a lot of corners to make a low cost GPU, and for the consumer they're not going to be worth it.

Economics 101.  AND this is why both Nvidia and AMD have taken so long to put out a "budget" GPU.

A 1650 Super costs about $500 USD right now.  YEAH SURE GREAT BUY!

Yes, once scalpers get a hold of this it's going to take it up to $300 - $400, but if you can get it directly from a retailer it's going to be $300 or less.  But, because of the low price scalpers will be buying this up like crazy so you're going to be in a constant struggle.  AMD isn't bothering making a lot of GPUs right now because the market is trash, and not just because of scalpers and mining, but also because of the EU countries putting a 20 - 25% VAT on these products, and the US putting a 25% tariff on them, and this DIRECTLY affects the MSRP, because the import companies pay that tax, and that's the companies, AMD, Nvidia, MSI, ASUS, XFX, Gigabyte, PowerColor, etc....  So they have to build that cost into their MSRP.  I don't know when EU countries threw in such a large VAT for GPUs coming out of China, which they all do, I know the US added it Jan 1, 2021.  They had actually added it a year or two earlier but had allowed exemptions up until that date.  The different companies gave press releases about it and said their prices were going up, and LTT covered how it not only affected the US but also Canada.

Steve never wants to admit this is affecting prices, but it is, and by a LOT, and no market escapes it even if that country doesn't charge such a high tax.  Add to that, it costs more to ship.  Add to that, to even make products now, it's about 15% more expensive than 2 years ago because of how badly inflation has hit the entire world.

So, if by 2023 AMD and Nvidia along with all their partners have pushed to have the assembly of GPUs moved out of China, then you'll see a drop in price.  The high inflation though, well 2022 is supposed to add ANOTHER 5 - 7% of inflation.  The only way for that to stop, and for there to be deflation, is a global recession and people aren't buying.

High quality APUs are going to come out with Zen 4, and Intel is going to do the same with 13th gen.  Low cost GPUs just aren't feasible with such large import taxes. CPUs and APUs don't come out of China and aren't subject to these large import taxes, and shipping costs are less per unit for a CPU or APU than for a GPU,  Weight, size?

This is why AMD and Nvidia have delayed putting out low end GPUs with RDNA 2 and Ampere.  It's too hard to meet market expectation while making the profit margin they need to make for it to be worth making, and for next gen parts it won't be any better.  Maybe by 2025 it will, if GPU assembly is out of China, and there'll be a lot more production capacity for ICs with a lot of fabs coming online for advanced nodes by then.


But making a statement that spending $500 USD for a product about the same as a product you might be able to find for $300 USD is just silly.  There is no such thing as a decent buy on a budget GPU, or any GPU, but at least at the high end people are used to paying more.

@mariom1674  You might want to upgrade your CPU at some point, but it certainly isn't necessary either. That being said, the net cost (including what you can get for selling your 1600) of upgrading to a 5600X, or a 3600, or perhaps a 5600G, wouldn't be all that much. A 5600X in particular would be very good for many more years to come, though you might also want to upgrade the memory as well in order to get the most out of it (depending on what you currently have right now). I'm assuming you're on a 300 series motherboard, but it looks like bios support is coming for Zen 3 (5000 series) CPUs, and is already here on some boards. I think there are also already some third party bioses for that, but you'd want to be extra careful before trying to use one of those.
